subject: Theoretical question: Guttman Scale -- IRT parameters are too high

messages.author: ea21f7bb0093ce5e
messages.subject: Theoretical question: Guttman Scale -- IRT parameters are too high
parts:
Dear Phil,
I always come here because I know this place have trusted information and you are very receptive of our questions and comments.

I am working on a project where children's parents assessed they children (daughters or sons) using a Likert scale within the framework of "model of hierarchical complexity". In other words, the items have an incremental complexity, such as "Without your showing him how, does your child scribble back and forth when you give him a crayon" and "After your child draws a “picture,” even a simple scribble, does your child tell you what she drew? ".  

To scoring key is 0 when children are not able to perform the specific behavior, 1 when they do the specific behavior sometimes, and 2 for always. Every child started with a specific starting item and we have no missing values in this dataset. We coded with "2" for all items with a lower complexity when a higher complexity item have received "2" and we coded with "0" for all items after three "0" in a row. 

I'm using the Samejima Graded Response Model to deal with the data and the model fit is ok :

            M2   df            p      RMSEA    RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95     SRMSR       TLI       CFI
stats 1646.653 1224 5.218048e-15 0.02121797 0.01847513 0.02380126 0.1241181 0.9968471 0.9969732


However, the "a" parameter is too high (e.g., 5.29 or even higher) and I'm struggling to explain why this is happening. Do you think the missing imputation strategy can be seen as causal to that?

Any idea.
The dataset is attached and I'm using the following basic code:
library(mirt)
mod <- mirt(cognitive, 1, itemtype = "graded", method = "MHRM")
M2(mod, type = "C2")
coef(mod, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)


Thank you

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Theoretical question: Guttman Scale -- IRT parameters are too high
parts:
Hi Luis,

It certainly seems to be the case that a Guttman scale would do fairly well in this data since the slopes for nearly all items are quite high (I used the EM algorithm default and noticed the same thing). I believe it's possible to estimate a probabilistic version of Guttman's scaling in mirt via the mdirt() function, but I don't have an example on hand. The sirt package demonstrates how this can be done with mirt using some of the customization features (https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/sirt/versions/2.7-50/topics/prob.guttman), but many of these discrete realizations have been absorbed into the mdirt() function for simplicity in specification. 

Note that the C2 statistic on the current CRAN release is slightly off. The dev version of Github contains the fix, which gives the following output (feel free to install to get this fix).
M2   df p      RMSEA    RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95      SRMSR      TLI     CFI

stats 3806.757 1224 0 0.05245096 0.05053475 0.05430834 0.09672008 0.989825    0.990232

Phil
